record.paper_title: Gamma-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. New discoveries and open questions
record.original_question: What physical and temporal connection links radio-band emission and gamma-ray emission in the radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies SBS 0846+513 and PMN J0948+0022, given that their gamma-ray flares and radio flares do not show similar behavior?

evidence.quote: A complex connection between the radio and γ-ray emission was observed for SBS 0846+513 and PMN J0948+0022, where γ-ray and radio flares have not a similar behaviour.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Consider the two radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies SBS 0846+513 and PMN J0948+0022, both of which are known gamma-ray emitters detected by the Fermi Large Area Telescope. Multiwavelength monitoring of these sources shows that their gamma-ray flares and their radio-band flares do not exhibit similar light-curve behavior (e.g., flares in one band are not simply contemporaneous or proportional to those in the other). Determine the physical mechanism and temporal relationship that connect the radio-band emission to the gamma-ray emission in these two sources. Specifically, identify (i) the emission region(s) responsible for each band (for instance, location along the relativistic jet relative to the central black hole and broad-line region), (ii) the radiative process(es) producing the gamma-rays (e.g., synchrotron self-Compton vs. external Compton on disk, broad-line, or torus photons) and the radio emission (synchrotron from compact, optically thick or thin jet components), and (iii) the expected sign and magnitude of the time lag between gamma-ray flares and the corresponding radio flares, together with an explanation of why a one-to-one correspondence between flares is not observed.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent multiwavelength studies (e.g., Foschini et al. 2015; D'Ammando et al. 2013–2020) have found that gamma-ray flares in SBS 0846+513 and PMN J0948+0022 are typically followed by delayed radio flares of the order of weeks to months, consistent with gamma-ray emission produced upstream of the radio "core" at 15–43 GHz. However, no unique, fully predictive model has been established, and the detailed location of the gamma-ray dissipation zone and the exact lag statistics remain debated, so the question is best characterized as partially understood but still open.

status_evidence.title: The first gamma-ray outburst of a radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy: the case of SBS 0846+513
status_evidence.snippet: D'Ammando et al. report a gamma-ray flare from SBS 0846+513 in 2011 followed by a delayed radio flare, suggesting the gamma-ray emission originates upstream of the radio emitting region.
status_evidence.claim: Gamma-ray flares in SBS 0846+513 lead radio flares by weeks–months, consistent with separate but causally connected emission zones.

status_evidence.title: Radio and gamma-ray follow-up of the exceptionally high-activity state of PMN J0948+0022 in 2013
status_evidence.snippet: The 2013 gamma-ray flare of PMN J0948+0022 was followed by a major radio outburst with a delay of several months, attributed to opacity effects and the relative position of emission regions along the jet.
status_evidence.claim: PMN J0948+0022 shows delayed radio response to gamma-ray flares, but the exact dissipation site remains under discussion.
